## The close surroundings of QX Pup: clump *S*

We have detected compact SiS ($v$=1, $J$=17-16), $^{30}$SiO ($v$=1, $J$=7-6), and Na$^{37}$Cl ($v$=0, $J$=26-25) emission arising *entirely* from clump *S* (Fig. [3](#f-compact)). Vibrationally excited SiS and SiO lines such as those observed here (with E$_{\rm u}$$\sim$1200-1800 K) are known to be produced in the warm inner ($\ensuremath{\lesssim}$10$^{15}$cm) layers of the winds of evolved mass-losing stars, where dust grain formation is probably not yet complete and where the stellar wind may have not reached its terminal expansion velocity (cite: hof18). This supports the hypothesis that clump *S* harbours QX Pup.

The region where the SiS $v$=1, $^{30}$SiO $v$=1, and Na$^{37}$Cl $v$=0 line emission is produced is barely resolved in our $\sim$0.2$''$-0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$3-resolution ALMA maps. We have fitted an elliptical gaussian to the integrated intensity maps of the SiS $v$=1 transition, which is the line with the highest signal-to-noise ratio, leading to a deconvolved angular diameter of the emitting source of $\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$08.

At a distance of $d$=1500 pc, this implies that the emission is confined to a small emitting volume of radius $\sim$60 AU ($\sim$24$R_{\star}$) comparable to that of the continuum-emitting core at the center, i.e., clump *S* (§ [3](#res-cont)).

The spectral profiles of these transitions, integrating the line surface brightness over the compact emitting area at clump *S*, are centered at $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$35 km s$^{-1}$ and have full widths at half maximum in the range FWHM$\sim$8-12 km s$^{-1}$ (Fig. [3](#f-compact), middle panel). These narrow profiles are consistent with low expansion velocities of $V_{\rm exp}$$\sim$5-7 km s$^{-1}$, adopting a Gaussian-like profile

and assuming isotropic mass-loss in these inner-wind regions.

(In case of a non-spherical mass distribution, for example if there is an equatorial density enhancement resulting in a torus or disk-like dominant emission component, the expansion velocity could be larger after taking into account line-of-sight projection effects).

The size and expansion velocity measured imply that the SiS $v$=1, $^{30}$SiO $v$=1, and Na$^{37}$Cl emission lines sample wind layers that have been ejected within the last $\sim$50 yr. The lines’ centroid ($V_{\rm sys}$=35 km s$^{-1}$) then represent the systemic velocity of the mass-losing star (QX Pup) averaged during the last 50 years.

The profile of the $^{30}$SiO ($v$=1, $J$=7-6) transition reported here is remarkably different from that of any of the known SiO maser lines detected in OH 231.8, which are characterized by two or three isolated $\sim$2-3 kms-wide, intense ($\approx$1-10 Jy) emission peaks (cite: san02; dod18). The different broader profile and the weakness of the $^{30}$SiO ($v$=1, $J$=7-6) line, with a peak intensity of only $\sim$17 mJy, points to thermal (i.e., non-maser) emission in this case.

## A compact bipolar outflow emerging from clump *S*

In addition to disclosing the locus of QX Pup (inside clump *S*), our ALMA data have also uncovered the existence of a compact ($\sim$1$''$$\times$4$''$) bipolar outflow that is emerging from the stellar vicinity.

This outflow is exclusively traced in our data by the SiO molecule, which is a well-known shock tracer.

Our SiO ($J$=7-6) and $^{29}$SiO ($J$=8-7) velocity-channel maps (Figs. [4](#f-sio) and [5](#f-29sio)) show very similar brightness distributions, both transitions displaying a notable bipolar morphology with two flame-shaped lobes

at either side of clump *S*. The SiO lobes are oriented along PA$\sim$16$^\circ$-18$^\circ$, that is, similarly but not totally equal to the large-scale CO outflow.

The emission is centered at $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$35 km s$^{-1}$, with most of the blue-shifted (down to $V_{\rm LSR}$=18 km s$^{-1}$) and red-shifted (up to $V_{\rm LSR}$=53 km s$^{-1}$) emission coming from the north and south SiO lobe, respectively. This is consistent with a dominant expansive kinematics centered at clump *S*.

The flame-shaped SiO lobes have a relative surface brightness dip at their respective centers suggestive of a dense-walled structure (this is best seen in the north lobe in the $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$29-30 km s$^{-1}$-channel maps of $^{29}$SiO ($J$=8-7), Fig. [5](#f-29sio)). Our SiO ($J$=7-6) maps show a pinched-waist emission distribution that is also hinted, but is less apparent, in the maps of the $^{29}$SiO ($J$=8-7) line.

From the maps of both transitions, SiO and $^{29}$SiO, we derive a similar size for the pinched-waist, which has a deconvolved half-intensity diameter of $\diameter_{\rm 1/2}$$\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$18$\sim$270 AU (as measured in the $V_{\rm LSR}$=35 km s$^{-1}$-channel map).

Unlike the large-scale CO outflow, the SiO emission distribution is rather (but not perfectly) symmetric about the nebular axis and the equator.

An `S`-shape distribution

is hinted, with both the east side of the north lobe and the west side of the south lobe being moderately brighter than its mirror image about the symmetry axis of the nebula.

Along the nebula axis, the SiO outflow reaches out to distances of $\sim$1.8$''$$\sim$2700 AU from the center,

with the north lobe being slightly brighter at the tips.

The dimensions of the outflow deduced from the maps of the weaker, optically thinner $^{29}$SiO ($J$=8-7) transition are moderately smaller along the nebula axis as a result of the lower signal-to-noise ratio of these maps.

The surface brightness distribution of SiO and $^{29}$SiO peaks at two diametrically opposed compact regions located at offsets $\delta$y$\sim$$\pm$0.11$''$ along the nebula axis (hereafter, referred to as SiO knots). This is most clearly seen in the position-velocity (PV) diagrams along the major axis of the bipolar outflow (Fig. [4](#f-sio) and [5](#f-29sio), bottom panels).

The distribution of the SiO emission increases abruptly from the center (offset 0$''$, $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$35 km s$^{-1}$) to the bright SiO knots, where the full width at zero-level intensity (FWZI) of the emission reaches a maximum value of $\sim$23 km s$^{-1}$.

This feature in the axial-PV diagram (i.e., abrupt velocity rise from the center to a compact region with the largest velocity-spread) is a well-known signature of bow-shocks. The latter are produced, for example, when a collimated fast wind or bullet collides with dense ambient material (cite: har87; lee03; bal13) and have been observed before in other pPNe, for example, in the molecular outflow of IRAS 22026+5306 (cite: sah06), in the ionized central regions of M 1-92 (cite: den08), and in the compact, shock-excited axial blobs or knots of Hen 3-1475 (cite: rie06). Analytical bow-shock models (cite: har87) as well as numerical computations (cite: den08) show that the FWZI of the emission profile produced by a radiating bow-shock equals the shock velocity, $V_{\rm s}$; this would imply that $V_{\rm s}$$\sim$23 km s$^{-1}$ for both the north and south bright SiO knots of OH 231.8. Using the simple analytic formula derived by (cite: har87), which relates the centroid of the bow-shock profile ($V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$29.5 and $\sim$41 km s$^{-1}$ at $\delta$y=+0.11$''$ and $\delta$y=$-$0.11$''$, respectively) with the shock-velocity, we deduce that the bow-shocks are viewed at an angle $i$$\sim$30$^\circ$ with respect to the plane of the sky, again similar but not the same as the large-scale outflow.

The axial PV diagram of SiO and $^{29}$SiO is somewhat structured and it is not possible to derive a unique velocity gradient from the center to the tips of the SiO lobes. The large velocities observed in the very inner regions of the outflow, near the SiO knots, are consistent with a large axial velocity gradient ranging between $\nabla \upsilonup$$\sim$85 and 50 km s$^{-1}$ arcsec$^{-1}$ (black dashed lines in Figs. [4](#f-sio) and [5](#f-29sio)). This gradient implies short kinematical ages of $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$\[84-142\]$\times$$\tan{(i)}$ years, that is, $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$50-80 yr adopting $i$=30$^\circ$ (or $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$60-100 yr, adopting the commonly used value of the inclination for the large-scale CO outflow, $i$=35$^\circ$).

The lower velocities at the intermediate-to-outer regions of the flame-shaped SiO lobes imply larger kinematic ages of $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$690$\times$$\tan{(i)}$ yr (about 400-500 yr, for $i$=30-35$^\circ$) and larger at the lobe tips. In these regions, however, the interpretation of the gradient is not straightforward since

it probably

involves

outflow deceleration from swept-up ambient material.

## The periphery of the SiO outflow

The close environments of the SiO outflow are remarkably disrupted. For example, this is clearly noticed in the $^{13}$CO (3-2) and CS (6-5) velocity-channel maps, and their respective axial PV diagrams, in regions within $\sim$$\pm$2$''$ from the center (Figs. [6](#f-pv-SiO-13co) and [20](#f-cs65)). These data show a surface brightness dip or minimum in the regions and LSR velocities where the SiO outflow is prominent. This suggests that the SiO outflow (perhaps jointly with an underlying powering wind not directly seen in these data)

is carving out the ambient material as it propagates outwards.

Since the expansion center of the SiO outflow (near clump *S*) is located about $\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$6 to the south of the waist’s center, the north SiO lobe is mainly colliding with, and piercing through, the slowly expanding equatorial waist (see $V_{\rm LSR}$=\[29:38\] km s$^{-1}$-channel maps in Fig. [6](#f-pv-SiO-13co)) whereas the south SiO lobe is colliding with the, presumably less dense, ambient material residing mainly in the base of the south large-scale lobe (and also partially in the south part of the waist).

In agreement with this wind-collision scenario, we identify a small-scale hourglass-shaped structure adjacent to the SiO outflow in the ALMA maps of most molecules.

This structure, dubbed as the mini-hourglass (or mini-hg), is nested inside the dense central regions of the large-scale nebula and is clearly recognized, for example, in the axial PV diagrams

shown in Figs. [6](#f-pv-SiO-13co)-[7](#f-miniw).

The mini-hg, and the two polar cavities inside, are also directly visible in the velocity-channel maps of most transitions near the systemic velocity, $V_{\rm LSR}$=35 km s$^{-1}$ (Fig. [7](#f-miniw), top-panel). We believe the walls of this hourglass-shaped structure are mainly made of compressed material formed as the SiO outflow propagates throughout the dense, central regions of the nebula.

The south lobe of the mini-hourglass, or south mini-lobe, can be traced (and is relatively well isolated from other nebular components) along the nebula axis down to $\delta$y$\sim$$-$1$''$ spanning the range of velocities $V_{\rm LSR}$=30-52 km s$^{-1}$. The south mini-lobe follows a velocity gradient similar to that of the outer regions of the south flame-shaped SiO lobe (dotted line in the axial PV diagrams of Fig. [6](#f-pv-SiO-13co) and [20](#f-cs65)). This suggests a similar age for both the extended flame-shaped SiO lobes and the mini-lobes ($t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$690$\times$$\tan{(i)}$ yr) or a similar dynamics.

The north mini-lobe is not so neatly delineated in our maps.

Yet, we clearly identify its central cavity (in the range $V_{\rm LSR}$=29-38 km s$^{-1}$) surrounded by very bright emission from the dense ambient material into which the SiO outflow is plowing.

The velocity gradient observed in the north mini-lobe is lower than in the south, as is also the case for the flamed-shaped lobes sampled by SiO and $^{29}$SiO emission. This is consistent with a larger resistance to the SiO outflow propagation toward the north (offered by the ambient material in the dense large waist) than toward the south, where the SiO outflow plunges into a presumably less dense ambient medium.

The equatorial waist of the compact mini-hourglass (referred to as the mini-waist) is partially resolved in our ALMA maps and is best isolated in the OCS (25-24) emission maps (Fig.[7](#f-miniw)), where we measure a full extent (at a $\sim$2$\sigma$ level) of $\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$35$\times$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$7, with the long axis oriented along PA$\sim$21+90$^\circ$.

This is consistent with a torus or disk-like structure with an outer radius of about 500 AU whose symmetry axis is viewed at an inclination angle of $i$$\sim$30$^\circ$, that is,

orthogonal to the SiO outflow (§ [4.2](#res-sio)).

The axial PV diagrams in Fig. [7](#f-miniw) show that south/north emission from the mini-waist (within $\delta y$$\pm$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$18) is blue-/red-shifted, that is, the velocity gradient has opposite sign to that observed along the mini-lobes, which is indicative of equatorial expansion.

The expansion velocity of the mini-waist is notably low and is not constant across the waist: it increases *linearly* from the inner to the outer regions (with values as low as \|$V_{\rm LSR}$-35\|$\sim$1 km s$^{-1}$ at the center and reaching \|$V_{\rm LSR}$-35\|$\sim$5 km s$^{-1}$ at the edges).

The gradient observed, $\nabla \upsilonup$$\sim$ 20-30 km s$^{-1}$ arcsec$^{-1}$, leads to a kinematical age for the equatorial mini-waist of $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$\[360-240\]/$\tan{(i)}$ years.

Assuming that the lobes and the waist of the mini-hourglass of OH 231.8 have the same kinematic age, as expected if both structures resulted from the same physical process (e.g., a sudden mass-loss ejection or mass-acceleration event), then we derive a value of the inclination of $i$$\sim$30$^\circ$-35$^\circ$ and a kinematical age of about 500 yr for these components.

*– The CH$_3$OH-outflow.* We have detected two transitions from methanol at 304.2 and 307.2 GHz (see Table [3](#t-lines) and Fig. [8](#f-ch3oh)). Their brightness distributions exhibit a clear bipolar morphology. The dimensions of the region where most of the CH$_3$OH emission is produced are similar to that of the compact SiO outflow. Weaker CH$_3$OH-emission components are also detected at larger distances from the center, up to $\sim$3-4$''$ along the nebula axis. The methanol emission profile is sharply peaked near $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$ 2, 29, 44 and 71 km s$^{-1}$, with extremely weak (undetected) emission at intermediate velocities.

The axial PV diagrams of the CH$_3$OH and $^{13}$CO ($J$=3-2) lines are plotted together in the bottom panels of Fig. [8](#f-ch3oh). In these diagrams, it is easy to see that the CH$_3$OH emission closely follows the spatio-kinematics of the mini-hourglass, neighboring the SiO outflow.

The CH$_3$OH emission is rather patchy, with the brightest emission arising in the front side of the north mini-lobe (at $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$29 km s$^{-1}$) and close to its tip.

## The large-scale nebula

### The hourglass-shaped structure

The $\sim$8$''$$\times$4$''$-sized hourglass nebula traced by the dust thermal continuum emission maps (§ [3](#res-cont) and Fig. [1](#f-cont)) is the dominant emission component of most of the species mapped in this work. In Fig. [9](#f-cs76) we present the velocity-channel maps of CS (7-6), one of the dense gas tracers observed by us with ALMA, where this component is clearly seen in the $V_{\rm LSR}$=\[$-$10:+80\]km s$^{-1}$ range. (See also the $^{13}$CO ($J$=3-2) and CS (6-5) maps already introduced showing the 4$''$$\times$4$''$ central regions of the hourglass, Fig. [6](#f-pv-SiO-13co) and Fig. [20](#f-cs65)).

The large-scale hourglass nebula (or large hg) encompasses the equatorial waist and the base of the bipolar lobes known from previous works[^4].

The unprecedented angular resolution of our ALMA maps shows that the bipolar lobes, at their base, are essentially large cavities (of $\sim$3$''$ in width) surrounded by $\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$5-wide walls with a nearly parabolic morphology. Our maps reveal a highly structured and non-uniform surface brightness distribution in the lobe walls and in the equatorial waist. As in the continuum maps, the east side of the large hg is much brighter than the west side.

The spatio-kinematic distribution of the large hg confirms an overall radial expansion with a linear velocity gradient along the nebula long axis (PA=21$^\circ$) of $\nabla \upsilonup$$\sim$6.0-6.5 km s$^{-1}$ arcsec$^{-1}$ (Fig. [9](#f-cs76)); the same gradient is preserved along the more distant, fastest regions of the large-scale lobes (§ [4.4.2](#res-hv)). This value of the gradient is consistent (within uncertainties) with that reported from previous studies (§ [1](#intro)).

Although the large equatorial waist is well resolved spatially and spectrally in our ALMA data, an accurate description of its morphology, dimensions, and kinematics is difficult. This is because the nebular equator is remarkably disrupted by the interaction with the SiO outflow, which has plowed into it from the south, and also because the waist is the region from where the highly-structured bipolar lobes emerge, and therefore the emission from different nebular structures and substructures, with complex kinematics, overlap. With these limitations in mind, the large-scale equatorial waist can be roughly described as an expanding cylindrical structure orthogonal to the bipolar lobes.

The centroid of the waist is located at offset $\sim$($-$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$05, 0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$6). The $^{13}$CO ($J$=3-2) PV cut along PA=21+90$^\circ$ (the equator) passing through the waist center is shown Fig. [10](#f-largew). The $^{13}$CO ($J$=3-2) line and the rest of transitions that sample the waist consistently point to a systemic velocity of $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$32-33 km s$^{-1}$, i.e., slightly different from that of clump *S* ($V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$35 km s$^{-1}$). The outer radius of the waist is $r_{\rm w}$$\sim$1$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$8 at a $\sim$2$\sigma$-level in the $^{13}$CO ($J$=3-2) maps (and slightly smaller, $r_{\rm w}$$\sim$1$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$4, in the maps of other less abundant molecules, e.g. CS). The waist extends about $\sim$$\pm$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$6 about its equator, but this is uncertain because there is not a sharp boundary separating the waist from the base of the lobes (probably, both are part of a unique hourglass-shaped structure). We identify a small cavity, of radius $\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$2-0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$25, at the center of the waist. From here, the emission increases quite sharply with the radius, reaching a peak at about $r$$\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$6-0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$7 and fading gradually at larger distances.

Toward the center of the waist, the radial velocity increases from \|$V_{\rm LSR}$-$V_{\rm sys}$\|$\sim$3 km s$^{-1}$ at the inner edge (immediately beyond the cavity) to about \|$V_{\rm LSR}$-$V_{\rm sys}$\|$\sim$25 km s$^{-1}$ at the outermost regions (Fig. [10](#f-largew)).

The waist layers at $r$$\sim$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$65 where the $^{13}$CO ($J$=3-2) emission peaks, are characterized by a radial velocity of \|$V_{\rm LSR}$-$V_{\rm sys}$\|$\sim$6-7 km s$^{-1}$. Adopting a cylindrical shape for the waist with its revolution axis inclined with respect to the sky-plane by $i$=35$^\circ$, this implies a deprojected velocity gradient of

about 10$\times$$\cos{(i)}$$\sim$8.2 km s$^{-1}$ arcsec$^{-1}$, leading to a kinematical age of $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$715 yr/$\cos{(i)}$$\sim$870 yr, similar to that of the large-scale outflow.

*Selective tracers of the waist.* The emission from certain molecular lines, namely, OCS ($J$=25-24), H$_3$O$^+$ ($J^p_K$=1$^-_1$ - 2$^+_{1}$), and SO$_2$ (11$_{6,6}$-12$_{5,7}$), is largely restricted to the $\sim$2$''$$\times$1$''$ central parts of the large hg (Fig. [11](#f-waist)).

Emission from OCS is observed over a relatively narrow velocity range ($V_{\rm LSR}$=\[18:42\] km s$^{-1}$) tracing selectively the equatorial $waist$ of the large hg and, also, of the compact mini-hg nested inside (see also Figs. [7](#f-miniw) and [21](#f-ocs)). This is probably because the relatively high-excitation requirements of this transition (E$_{\rm u}$$\sim$190 K) are not attained at large distances along the fast lobes, which are predominantly cold (§ [5.1](#s-rd)).

The SO$_2$ emission maps resemble those of OCS, which is probably explained by the similar upper-level energy of both transitions (Table [3](#t-lines)).

The surface brightness distribution of H$_3$O$^+$ is slightly more extended, rounded, and uniform than that of OCS and SO$_2$.

This is consistent with this ion being mainly a product of the photodissociation chain of H$_2$O and CO by the interstellar UV radiation in the outer layers of the envelope (cite: san15).

As OCS, the H$_3$O$^+$ and SO$_2$ transitions have also some contribution to the emission produced in the mini-waist.

### The high-velocity bipolar lobes

The high-velocity (HV) bipolar lobes are, after the large hg, the second major component of the molecular outflow of OH 231.8 (§ [1](#intro)). In our ALMA maps, the $^{12}$CO (3-2) emission from the north and south lobe reaches out to radial distances of $\sim$17$''$ and $\sim$30$''$, respectively, along the PA$\sim$21$^\circ$ axis (Fig. [12](#f-12co)). The lobes are also traced by a number of molecules other than $^{12}$CO (Table [\[t-sketch\]](#t-sketch)). These species, with emission lines substantially fainter than $^{12}$CO ($J$=3-2), trace only certain parts of the lobes (normally, the CO-brightest regions).

The HV bipolar lobes are highly structured, and a number of nested, often incomplete, substructures appear to be present; some of these are counterparts of major

features identified in the optical and near-IR images of OH 231.8 (skirt, spine, fingers, filaments, etc – see (cite: buj02; mea03; bal17)).

All these substructures are characterized by a dominant expansive kinematics described by a radial velocity gradient, $\nabla \upsilonup$$\sim$6.0-6.5 km s$^{-1}$ arcsec$^{-1}$, that is sustained from the base (i.e., low-latitude regions of the large hg) to the tips of the lobes where the highest *los*-velocities are observed, (\|$V_{\rm LSR}$-$V_{\rm sys}$\|$\sim$125 and $\sim$200 km s$^{-1}$ for the north and south lobes, respectively – Fig. [13](#f-co-pvs)). The kinematic age of the HV-bipolar lobes implied by this velocity gradient is $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$1150$\times$$\tan{(i)}$, that is, $t_{\rm kin}$$\sim$800 yr for $i$=35$^\circ$.

## NEW macro-structures unveiled by ALMA: the fish bowls

The unprecedented sensitivity of the ALMA maps reported here has enabled us to detect for the first time the molecular counterpart of the two faint, rounded structures seen in the $HST$/NIR images toward the central regions of OH 231.8$+$4.2 (Fig. [12](#f-12co)). Curiously, no previous published studies of these dusty structures exist to date (to our knowledge). These components are best identified in the $^{12}$CO ($J$=3-2) velocity-channel maps shown in Fig. [14](#f-calamardos) where they appear as elliptical, ring-like emission features around the bright central regions of the nebula. We refer to these structures as the fish bowls.

The northern fish bowl ($FB_{\rm N}$) can be relatively well isolated from

other (lobe and waist) line-emitting regions in the velocity range $V_{\rm LSR}$=\[$-$13:+59\] km s$^{-1}$. It comes into sight as a compact elongated emission feature at offset ($-$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$6, 0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$75) in the $V_{\rm LSR}$=$-$13 km s$^{-1}$ channel. As $V_{\rm LSR}$ increases, this feature progressively grows and develops an elliptical ring-like morphology that reaches a maximum size of $\sim$8$''$$\times$6$''$ (with the long axis oriented along PA$\sim$125$^\circ$) in channels near the centroid of the $FB_{\rm N}$-emission profile, $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$23-26 km s$^{-1}$.

As $V_{\rm LSR}$ continues increasing, the ring-shaped emitting region steadily shrinks and dims,

turning into a faint compact emission clump, located at offset (0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$2, 3$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$6), in channel $V_{\rm LSR}$$\sim$59 km s$^{-1}$.

The ring-like feature appears clearly incomplete in several central channels, in particular, a vast part of the northern rim emission is missing at $V_{\rm LSR}$$\leq$41 km s$^{-1}$.

The southern fish bowl ($FB_{\rm S}$)

comes out as a faint and compact elongated emission region at $V_{\rm LSR}$=+77 km s$^{-1}$ (at offset $-$0$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$8, 1$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$4) that progressively becomes larger, brighter, and acquires a ring-like morphology as the velocity decreases. This feature reaches maximum dimensions of $\sim$8$''$$\times$6$''$ (with the long axis oriented along PA$\sim$100$^\circ$) in channels around $V_{\rm LSR}$=47 km s$^{-1}$. As the velocity continues decreasing, the size of the ring-like emission feature reduces. The $FB_{\rm S}$-emission can be discerned down to $V_{\rm LSR}$=17 km s$^{-1}$, but only from the west side. At lower LSR velocities, the line-wing emission from the $FB_{\rm S}$ (expected to be faint and compact, if any) cannot be isolated or disentangled from the intense emission produced in the south lobe near its base. As its northern analog, the $FB_{\rm S}$ appears incomplete or broken, particularly, its the southern rim.

The simplest configuration that is consistent with the observed spatio-kinematic distribution of the $^{12}$CO ($J$=3-2) emission from the fish bowls is a pair of hollow, thin-walled ellipsoids radially expanding. The projection of the outer surface of these ellipsoids in the plane of the sky is represented by the ellipses overplotted on the $^{12}$CO ($J$=3-2) integrated intensity maps (Figure [14](#f-calamardos), bottom panels).

A three-dimensional view of a generic ellipsoid, with semi-major axes $a$, $b$, and $c$, is given in Fig. [15](#f-elipse) (left) as well as a cut of it through the $ac$-plane, which contains the *los*  (Fig. [15](#f-elipse), middle). As we will see below, the sizes of $b$ and $a$ can be constrained from the observations, however, $c$ is uncertain since this axis can be tilted with respect to the *los* by a given (unknown) inclination angle $i_{\rm c}$ (Fig. [15](#f-elipse), right).

For radial expansion, the velocity-channel maps (Figure [14](#f-calamardos)) offer a sliced view of the emitting volume intersected by different planes perpendicular to the *los*. Therefore, the channels near the systemic velocity ($V_{\rm sys}$$\sim$23-26 and $\sim$47 km s$^{-1}$ for the $FB_{\rm N}$ and $FB_{\rm S}$, respectively) represent the cross-sectional cut of the ellipsoids through their expansion center. This is indeed consistent with the fact that the largest ring-like emitting areas are observed near $V_{\rm sys}$ and enable us to estimate $b$$\sim$4$.\!\!^{\prime\prime}$1 (for both fish bowls).
